newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: European feed trade awaits USDA estimate for clues.
newsitem.headline: European feed trade awaits USDA estimate for clues.

text.p: European physical feed players are eagerly awaiting the latest USDA estimate of the 1996/97 soybean carry-over due on Thursday this week, which should give a more concrete clue to near-term market direction, they say.
In the meantime, a dollar/mark rate around 1.72 continues to act as a brake on fresh trade at such a time of uncertainty. There was no European business reported early on Monday.
"People are looking to the USDA figure and we could see some heavy long liquidation after that," said analyst Arie van Dijk of market statisticians Stigevo.

"More and more people are thinking the carry-over figure will be increased and if you look at the longs on July (futures in Chicago), we could see that position down below eight dollars (a bushel)," he said. "That will depress sentiment in Europe and we won't see much business until then."
The July soybean futures contract on the Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT) closed on Friday at 8.35-1/2 a bushel. On Project A trade overnight, it touched a low of $8.21.
Many market watchers had expected the USDA to lower the figure last month but it unexpectantly left it unchanged at 125 million bushels.
European soymeal prices are already down around 20 percent in the last few weeks and buying interest is still low. Traders are wondering when the market will bottom out.

Van Dijk said he expected the Chicago July position to come down as low as $7.60 but any further would spark Asian demand, causing a price bounce. Traders in Asia have said they would consider entering the market if July reached $7.20.
"It will stop the price getting to $7.00," Van Dijk said.

Elsewhere, nearby tapioca should continue to see some business this week, following the delayed arrival of one vessel, the Ziya K, to northwestern Europe, believed to be carrying 25,000 tonnes if tapioca. Traders said there may be some additional cover taken in Europe this week.
But traders also point out that there will be heavier arrivals of the product from the end of this month, which will co-incide with increased demand for tapioca.
"Grains are still too expensive for pig feed and we will see maximum incorporation of tapioca," Van Dijk said.
He said that despite an estimated 30 percent drop in overall pig feed demand due to swine fever, tapioca usage should increase. "We will see a very sound tapioca market," he said.
